A public notice board offers ordinary paid work, overseen by a local work organiser. A lantern hangs beside it. The low boundary wall bears the last flood's silt stripe and caught leaves; the board was moved uphill. A bell near the board has a finger-length crack rising from its lower lip, a small chip missing along one edge, and dirt within the break. Its clapper can strike the damaged section. The organiser warns that ringing it will bring people to investigate.

result.summary: 3 minutes pass (Inspecting the bell's split rim by lantern light.)

narration:
The split starts at the bell’s lower lip and runs upward for about a finger’s length. Tali stands beside you, keeping the lantern’s light on the rim.

From the outside, the damage looks like a single crack. Looking beneath the lip reveals a small chip missing from one edge. Dirt has settled into the break; it isn’t a clean, freshly exposed surface. That tells you it has been there a while—not what caused it.

The clapper hangs close enough to strike the damaged section. You can inspect it without sounding the bell, but testing the bell’s voice would be another matter.

“Would it still carry across the water?” Tali asks, leaning a little closer without touching it.

Behind you, the work organiser looks over from the notices. “If you’re going to ring that, say so first. People will come looking.”

For now, the square remains quiet.

narration:
Oren points downhill. “If you mean the barrier access, the narrow bridge is that way. Mind the board at the entrance.”

Beyond the square’s low wall, a short plank bridge crosses a drainage channel to a closed maintenance gate. Its warning board reads: **UNSAFE DECK — NO PUBLIC ACCESS.** One handrail sags; near the middle, a plank has split around its fastening. Water slides past the stonework below.

You approach the first boards, testing your weight before committing to the crossing. Getting across will mean keeping to the supported edges and negotiating the damaged section; a slip could leave you hanging over the channel. The gate beyond is a separate obstacle.

The first boards hold. At the damaged section, a fastening pulls loose with a sharp squeal.

The plank tips beneath your foot. You drop hard against the edge, catching a supporting beam with both hands as the loose timber splashes into the channel. Cold water washes over your boots. The sagging handrail hangs above you, beyond easy reach.

You have not reached the gate. Your grip holds for now, but there is no deck directly beneath you. On the square side, an exposed crossbeam sits within reach of one foot—a possible foothold for climbing back, if you can shift your weight onto it.

From uphill, Oren calls, “Keep off the rail! The post’s coming out!”

**What do you do?**

From beneath the broken deck, you can see the downstream stonework almost at water level. Looking costs you no handhold, but the bridge support blocks part of the view.

A pale horizontal cut crosses the face of one stone just above the water. Unlike the irregular mortar joints, it stops short of the stone’s edges. There’s a smaller vertical nick at its centre. It looks deliberately made.

No number or lettering is visible from here. It could be a reference mark, but without its recorded height—or another known point to compare it with—you cannot turn it into a water-level measurement. A dark band of wet stone extends above it; passing ripples alternately cover and expose the cut.

Your arms are still bearing your weight. The square-side crossbeam remains within reach of a boot; examining the mark more closely would mean first finding secure support.
